questions.question: How should nitric acid containers be stacked?

options.text: Stack no more than two containers high.
Stack them all the way to the ceiling.
Load them on top of other products.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stack no more than two containers high.
questions.explanation: Nitric acid containers can be stacked, but only two containers high maximum. Never stack them on top of other products.

questions.question: What is the correct way to check tire pressure?

options.text: Push on the tires with your hand.

questions.explanation: You must check your tires before each trip. The only way to accurately check tire pressure is with a tire pressure gauge.

questions.question: What do you need to know to decide which placards to use for hazardous materials?

options.text: The hazard classes of the materials.
The types of containers being used.

questions.correctAnswerText: The hazard classes of the materials.
questions.explanation: Placards on a vehicle show the hazard classes of the materials being carried. You must know the hazard class to choose the correct placard.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a hazardous material?
questions.explanation: Hazardous materials are things that pose risks during transport. These include explosives, flammable gases, and hazardous solids. Rocks are not considered hazardous materials.

questions.question: What is the right way to check tire pressure?

options.text: Push on the tire with your hand.
Measure how tall the tire is.

questions.explanation: Check your tires at the start of each trip and after every stop. A tire pressure gauge is the only way to check tire pressure correctly.

questions.question: Where should hazardous materials shipping papers NOT be kept?

options.text: In a pouch on the driver's side door.
In a pouch on the passenger's side door.
Within reach of the driver while wearing a seat belt.
On the driver's seat when the driver is outside the vehicle.

questions.correctAnswerText: In a pouch on the passenger's side door.
questions.explanation: Keep shipping papers in a pouch on the driver's door or within reach of the driver while driving. If you leave the vehicle, put papers on the driver's seat. Never put them on the passenger's side door.

questions.question: When loading hazardous materials, which of these should you NOT do?
questions.explanation: Do not use hooks or tools that could damage containers or packaging when loading hazardous materials.

questions.question: When transporting mass explosives, what is required?

options.text: The vehicle must always have placards.
Placards are only needed if carrying more than 200 pounds.
The vehicle does not need placards.

questions.correctAnswerText: The vehicle must always have placards.
questions.explanation: Some hazardous materials only need placards if 1,001 pounds or more are being carried. Mass explosives always require placards, no matter the amount.

questions.question: When refueling a vehicle that carries hazardous materials, what should you do?

options.text: Have someone other than the driver do it.

questions.explanation: Always turn off the engine before refueling a vehicle with hazardous materials. Someone must always stay at the nozzle to control the fuel.

questions.question: What license do you need to drive a vehicle carrying hazardous materials?

options.text: A CDL with a hazardous materials endorsement.
A CDL with a passenger endorsement.
A CDL with an air brake endorsement.

questions.correctAnswerText: A CDL with a hazardous materials endorsement.
questions.explanation: You must have a CDL with a hazardous materials endorsement to drive any vehicle used for transporting hazardous materials, even if it is not carrying hazardous materials at that time.

questions.question: What should a carrier do if hazardous materials are not properly prepared?

options.text: Accept the shipment, but make a note on the paperwork

questions.explanation: A carrier must refuse shipments of hazardous materials that are not properly prepared.

questions.question: How many hazardous materials classes are there?
questions.explanation: There are nine classes of hazardous materials. Each class shows the dangers of that type of material.

questions.question: When carrying Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, a vehicle should not be parked:
questions.explanation: When carrying Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, do not park within 300 feet of a bridge, tunnel, or building. Do not park near places where people gather or near open fire, except for brief stops to address vehicle needs.

questions.question: A person watching the loading or unloading of a tank must do all of the following, except:

options.text: Stay within 25 feet of the tank
Know the dangers of the materials

questions.explanation: A qualified supervisor must be present during loading or unloading. The supervisor must stay alert, watch the tank clearly, stay within 25 feet, know the material dangers, know emergency procedures, and be able to move the tank if needed.

questions.question: When transporting chlorine, what must be in the vehicle?
questions.explanation: A driver carrying chlorine in cargo tanks must keep an approved gas mask and an emergency kit in the vehicle.

questions.question: When transporting radioactive materials, it is important to know that:

options.text: Radiation passes through to other nearby packages
The packages should be carried in the cab
The packages should be laid on their side

questions.correctAnswerText: Radiation passes through to other nearby packages
questions.explanation: Radiation from radioactive packages passes through to other nearby packages. For this reason, only a limited number of radioactive packages can be loaded together.

questions.question: How must a shipper tell a driver about cargo risks?

options.text: By writing a note on blank paper
By putting hazard warning labels on packages
By placing orange dots on packages

questions.correctAnswerText: By putting hazard warning labels on packages
questions.explanation: Shippers must alert drivers and others to hazards using shipping papers, hazard warning labels on packages, emergency response information, and placards.

questions.question: When loading or unloading explosive materials, you should:

options.text: Use sharp tools to open packages

questions.explanation: Always turn off the engine before loading or unloading explosives. Never drop, throw, or roll packages with explosives.

questions.question: An improperly placarded vehicle can only be moved:

options.text: To make room for other vehicles

questions.explanation: A vehicle must have proper placards before driving. An improperly placarded vehicle can only be moved if necessary to protect life or property in an emergency.

questions.question: When driving a vehicle with empty hazardous materials cargo tanks, the driver:

options.text: Can cross railroad tracks without slowing or stopping
Must slow down at railroad tracks but is not required to stop
Must stop at railroad crossings before proceeding
Should never drive over railroad tracks

questions.correctAnswerText: Must stop at railroad crossings before proceeding
questions.explanation: A vehicle with hazardous materials cargo tanks must stop at railroad crossings before crossing, even if the tanks are empty.

questions.question: Besides reading the manual, what is the best way to learn about transporting hazardous materials?
questions.explanation: The manual teaches you what you need to pass the test. But it does not cover everything you need to know to do the job safely. Training courses give you more complete information.

questions.question: You notice hazardous materials leaking while driving. What should you do?

options.text: Park the vehicle as soon as possible.
Leave the area to find help.
Drive around looking for someone to repair the leak.

questions.correctAnswerText: Park the vehicle as soon as possible.
questions.explanation: If cargo leaks while you are driving hazardous materials, stop driving as soon as it is safe. Driving farther will make the contaminated area larger. Park the vehicle, secure the area, and have someone else get help while you stay with the vehicle.

questions.question: When transporting Division 1.1 materials, what should the floor liner be made of?
questions.explanation: Use a floor lining when transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 materials. The floors must be tight. The liner must be made of non-metallic material or metal without iron.

questions.question: Flammable gases are what class of hazard?
questions.explanation: Flammable gases are Class 2 hazardous materials.

questions.question: Where should placards be placed on a truck?

options.text: On the left and right sides.

questions.explanation: When hazardous materials placards are required, place them on all four sides of the vehicle.

questions.question: What does RQ stand for?
questions.explanation: When marking hazardous materials in an "HM" column on shipping papers, you can write "RQ" instead of "X" to show a reportable quantity of that material.

questions.question: When you are not in your vehicle, where should hazardous materials shipping papers be kept?
questions.explanation: Shipping papers must be easy to find. When you are not in your vehicle, leave hazardous materials shipping papers on the driver's seat.

questions.question: How should hazardous materials be loaded and unloaded?
questions.explanation: Heat can make many hazardous materials more dangerous. Load and unload hazardous materials away from heat sources.

questions.question: If a shipping paper lists both hazardous and non-hazardous materials, how can you tell them apart?

options.text: Non-hazardous materials are written in pencil.
Hazardous materials are listed in red ink.

questions.explanation: When a shipping paper lists both hazardous and non-hazardous materials, you can tell them apart in three ways. List hazardous materials first, highlight them in a different color, or mark them with an "X" in a column labeled "HM."

questions.question: What is a Class 7 hazardous material?
questions.explanation: Radioactive materials are Class 7 hazardous materials.
